result: Nine stable transgenic zebrafish lines were generated for targeted opsin expression using the GAL4/UAS binary expression system, with opsins fused to fluorescent protein reporters (tdTomato or eYFP).
evaluation: Claim C1 is directly supported by explicit statements in the manuscript and Figure 1A showing the list of generated opsin lines. The generation of stable transgenic lines is a core methodological achievement of the study, with detailed cloning and transgenesis protocols provided in the Materials and methods section.

result: In embryonic trigeminal neuron activation assays, CoChR showed the highest response probability with blue light (65-100% at 112-445 μW/mm2), ChrimsonR was the only cation channelrhodopsin responsive to amber light (~70% at 322 μW/mm2), and GtACR1/GtACR2 showed differential spectral responses consistent with their absorption spectra.
evaluation: Claims C2-C4 are supported by quantitative behavioral data presented in Figure 2F,G with specific response probabilities at defined irradiance levels. The spectral selectivity observations are consistent with known opsin properties cited from prior literature (Klapoetke et al., 2014; Govorunova et al., 2015).

result: In larval motor neuron activation assays, CoChR elicited tail movements with the highest probability and shortest latency using blue light (96-100% at 0.63-2.55 mW/mm2), while only ChrimsonR responded to red light (~78% at 1 mW/mm2).
evaluation: Claims C5-C6 are supported by quantitative behavioral data in Figure 3F,G showing response probabilities across irradiance levels. The spectral selectivity of ChrimsonR for red light is consistent with its known red-shifted absorption spectrum.

result: In vivo whole-cell recordings from primary motor neurons revealed that CoChR and ChrimsonR generated the largest photocurrents (475±186 pA and 251±73 pA respectively), Chronos showed the fastest deactivation kinetics (4.3±0.4 ms), and opsin expression did not alter basic physiological properties of neurons.
evaluation: Claims C7, C8, and C32 are supported by quantitative electrophysiological data in Figures 4B,C,E,G with appropriate statistical descriptors (mean±SD, sample sizes). The lack of effect on physiological properties (membrane resistance, resting potential, capacitance) provides important validation that opsin expression itself does not compromise neuronal function.

result: CoChR and ChrimsonR were the only opsins capable of inducing action potentials in primary motor neurons, with CoChR inducing spikes in all tested neurons (11/11 cells) with 5 ms pulses, ChrimsonR supporting firing up to 100 Hz with single spikes per pulse, CoChR producing spike bursts even with short pulses, and both opsins achieving short latency (3-4 ms) and low jitter (0.25-1.25 ms).
evaluation: Claims C9-C12 and C37 are supported by detailed electrophysiological data in Figure 5 with exact cell counts and quantitative measurements of spike timing. The differential performance characteristics between CoChR (burst firing) and ChrimsonR (single spikes, high-frequency fidelity) are well-documented with supporting data.

result: In embryonic behavioral suppression assays, GtACRs achieved the strongest suppression of coil rate with blue light (90-95% decrease at 8.4-225 μW/mm2), while GtACR1, eArch3.0, and eNpHR3.0 showed comparable suppression with amber light (80-90% decrease at 50.5-227 μW/mm2).
evaluation: Claims C13-C14 are supported by quantitative behavioral data in Figure 6F,G showing dose-dependent suppression across different wavelengths. The high efficacy of GtACRs is consistent with their large photocurrent amplitudes measured electrophysiologically.

result: In larval swim suppression assays, GtACR1, GtACR2, and eArch3.0 reduced bout rate with blue light (GtACRs achieving 20-45% decrease), while only eNpHR3.0 reduced bout rate with red light (45% decrease at 1 mW/mm2).
evaluation: Claims C15-C16 are supported by quantitative behavioral data in Figure 7D-F. The spectral selectivity and relative efficacy of different inhibitory opsins are well-documented, though the magnitude of suppression is more modest than in embryonic assays.

result: Electrophysiological characterization of inhibitory opsins revealed that GtACR1 photocurrents reversed 5-10 mV positive to ECl and were primarily chloride-driven, GtACRs generated photocurrents 3-10 times larger than Cl-/H+ pumps, GtACRs had the fastest activation kinetics (~1 ms), while Cl-/H+ pumps showed 2-10 times faster deactivation (14-22 ms eNpHR3.0, 27-37 ms eArch3.0), and anion channelrhodopsins induced inward currents while pumps generated outward currents.
evaluation: Claims C17-C20, C50-C51 are supported by detailed voltage-clamp data in Figure 8 and supplementary figures. The reversal potential analysis (C17) appropriately accounts for liquid junction potential and access resistance errors. The comparative kinetics measurements provide quantitative basis for understanding functional differences between channels and pumps.

result: GtACRs and eNpHR3.0 effectively inhibited action potentials in primary motor neurons (80-95% suppression of single spikes, 60-100% complete suppression of tonic firing at 10 mW/mm2), with GtACR1 capable of inhibiting even when using embryonic ECl conditions.
evaluation: Claims C21-C22 and C57 are supported by quantitative current-clamp data in Figure 9F-H showing inhibition efficacy across different stimulation protocols. The ability of GtACR1 to inhibit even with high ECl demonstrates that shunting mechanisms can overcome depolarizing chloride currents during sustained activation.

result: Anion channelrhodopsins (GtACRs) induced excitatory effects in embryonic neurons, including escape responses at light onset and transient spiking in primary motor neurons when using intracellular solutions mimicking embryonic ECl (-50 mV), consistent with GtACRs functioning as chloride-conducting channels in neurons with depolarized chloride reversal potential.
evaluation: Claims C28, C41, C54-C55, and C80 are supported by convergent behavioral (Figures 2, 6) and electrophysiological (Figure 9A) evidence. The developmental stage-specific excitatory effects are mechanistically explained by the high intracellular chloride concentration in immature neurons, making ECl more positive than resting potential. This interpretation is consistent with cited literature on developmental changes in chloride homeostasis (C49).

result: The combined behavioral and electrophysiological approach provided complementary insights for opsin tool selection, with behavioral assays enabling efficient evaluation across cell types and developmental stages, electrophysiological recordings affording quantitative calibration at single-cell resolution, and good qualitative agreement between approaches with behavioral efficacy predicting photocurrent amplitude rank order.
evaluation: Claims C58-C62 are supported by the overall study design and comparative analysis across Figures 2-10. The correlation between behavioral efficacy and photocurrent amplitude (C61, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) validates the utility of high-throughput behavioral screening. However, the claim of 'good qualitative agreement' should be interpreted cautiously as some opsins showed behavioral effects without inducing spikes in pMNs (C67).

result: Photocurrent amplitude in primary motor neurons was proportional to opsin expression level and predictive of behavioral induction efficacy (CoChR > ChrimsonR > ChR2(H134R) > Chronos ≥ CheRiff), with CoChR evoking spikes in all tested pMNs and triggering maximal behavioral responses at irradiances as low as 0.63 mW/mm2.
evaluation: Claims C72-C74 are supported by the correlation analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and behavioral/electrophysiological data throughout. The proportionality between expression and photocurrent (C72) and the predictive relationship to behavior (C73) provide important validation of the approach, though the correlation is based on a limited number of opsins (4 tdTomato-linked cation channels).

result: In primary motor neurons, light pulses can induce spike bursts and firing rate adaptation during high-frequency stimulation, likely due to plateau potentials and sodium channel inactivation, with CoChR being prone to burst firing even with short (0.5 ms) pulses that compromised high-frequency entrainment, while ChrimsonR showed less adaptation and fewer bursts despite lower overall efficacy.
evaluation: Claims C75-C76 and C79 are supported by detailed analysis of spiking patterns in Figure 5. The mechanistic interpretation (plateau potentials, sodium channel inactivation) is reasonable inference based on known neurophysiology, though not directly tested. The cell-type-specific limitations of CoChR are important caveats appropriately acknowledged by the authors.

result: Broad variation in opsin efficacy across lines was observed, likely attributable to differences in intrinsic opsin properties and variation in expression/membrane targeting, with membrane trafficking influenced by the fluorescent protein fusion partner, and better expression observed with tdTomato compared to tagRFP fusions.
evaluation: Claims C63-C65 are supported by the expression analysis in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, showing variable expression levels and membrane localization across lines. The inference about causes of variation (C63) is reasonable given the data, and the observation about tdTomato vs tagRFP (C65) is an empirical finding from the authors' experience, though not systematically tested in this study.

result: Although several opsin lines did not evoke action potentials in low-input-resistance primary motor neurons, behavioral assays showed all lines induced tail movements in larvae, likely due to recruitment of higher-input-resistance secondary motor neurons, and behavioral assays at multiple developmental stages revealed developmental-specific effects that were corroborated by electrophysiological recordings using solutions mimicking age-appropriate intracellular chloride concentrations.
evaluation: Claims C67-C68 are supported by the discrepancy between electrophysiological (Figure 5) and behavioral (Figure 3) results, with the explanation about secondary motor neurons being a reasonable inference supported by cited literature (Menelaou and McLean, 2012). The developmental validation using different ECl solutions (C68) demonstrates methodological rigor in linking behavioral and electrophysiological observations.

result: Some opsins showed higher response probability in transient versus stable transgenic animals (CheRiff, CoChR, GtACRs), likely due to higher expression levels, and no significant irradiance-dependent modulation of photocurrent amplitude was observed in cation channelrhodopsins, likely due to the high irradiance range tested.
evaluation: Claims C29 and C33 are supported by comparison of transient (Figure 2F) and stable (Figure 2G) expression data, and by photocurrent measurements across irradiance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F). The inferences about expression levels (C29) and irradiance saturation (C33) are reasonable explanations, though alternative mechanisms are not ruled out.

result: Longer tail movements (>100 ms, 4-5 cycles) observed in response to single light pulses indicate engagement of spinal central pattern generators, which may occur through recruitment of glutamatergic V2a interneurons connected via gap junctions and/or proprioceptive feedback via cerebrospinal fluid-contacting neurons.
evaluation: Claim C30 is supported by behavioral observations in Figure 3D showing prolonged movements, and the inference about central pattern generator engagement is reasonable. However, C31 is speculative, citing possible mechanisms from literature without direct experimental evidence in this study. The proposed mechanisms are plausible but not tested here.

result: Light exposure suppressed coiling behavior in opsin-expressing embryos followed by synchronized restart at light offset, with light also decreasing coiling in control embryos but to a significantly lesser degree, and optogenetically-evoked suppression likely resulting from distinct mechanisms in different transgenic lines.
evaluation: Claims C40 and C42 are supported by behavioral data in Figure 6D-G, with appropriate controls and statistical comparisons. The inference about distinct mechanisms (C43) is reasonable given the different ion selectivities and kinetics of the opsins, though the specific mechanisms are not directly tested in this result.

result: Opsin-negative larvae showed a 20-30% increase in bout rate during blue light illumination, no increase in bout rate was found in larvae expressing anion channelrhodopsins even during the initial 2 s suggesting GtACRs do not induce excitatory effects at larval stages, and motor neuron-specific expression resulted in decreased bout speed (~20%) but not bout rate.
evaluation: Claims C46-C48 are supported by behavioral data in Figure 7 and supplementary figures. The observation about control larvae (C46) is consistent with prior literature (Andalman et al., 2019). The lack of excitatory effects in larvae (C47) contrasts with embryonic results and is appropriately analyzed. The cell-type-specific effects (C48) provide insight into circuit-level mechanisms.

result: All opsins except eNpHR3.0 showed bi-phasic photocurrent responses with fast activation followed by slow inactivation, likely due to opsin transitioning to an inactive state, while Cl-/H+ pumps showed little inactivation (600-1000 ms for eArch3.0).
evaluation: Claims C52-C53 are supported by voltage-clamp recordings in Figure 8B,F. The mechanistic interpretation of bi-phasic kinetics (C52) is supported by cited literature on opsin photocycles (Chow et al., 2010; Mattis et al., 2011; Schneider et al., 2015). The quantitative measurements of inactivation kinetics are clearly presented.

result: Data from eArch3.0-expressing neurons could not be collected in later protocol stages due to recording degradation or cell depolarization, suggesting repeated eArch3.0 activation may alter neuronal electrical properties.
evaluation: Claim C56 describes an experimental limitation and proposes a mechanistic explanation supported by a citation (Williams et al., 2019). However, the inference that repeated activation causes the problem is uncertain as alternative explanations (e.g., recording stability issues, phototoxicity) are not ruled out. This is an important caveat for eArch3.0 use but requires further investigation.

result: The transient nature of GtACR-induced spiking and motor activity might be due to initial large inward photocurrent depolarizing neurons above threshold, similar to observations in rat cortical and cultured hippocampal neurons attributed to antidromic spiking from positively shifted axonal ECl, suggesting GtACR use in immature neurons or subcellular structures should be carefully calibrated with Cl-/H+ pumps potentially preferable.
evaluation: Claim C81 is speculative about the mechanism underlying transient effects. C82 cites relevant observations from other systems (Malyshev et al., 2017; Mahn et al., 2018) but these may not directly apply to zebrafish motor neurons. The recommendation in C83 is reasonable given the observed developmental effects, but the preference for pumps over channels is not systematically tested in this study.

result: The mechanism of GtACR-mediated silencing is likely shunting due to large photocurrents reducing input resistance, with potential additional contribution from depolarization block depending on physiological ECl, and GtACRs' large photocurrents with fast activation kinetics explain their efficacy in inhibiting single action potentials, while Cl-/H+ pumps' fast deactivation kinetics allowed rapid resumption of spiking at light offset, with kinetic differences between channels and pumps potentially affecting temporal resolution of inhibition and recovery.
evaluation: Claims C84-C88 are supported by the photocurrent measurements (Figure 8) and spike inhibition data (Figure 9). The mechanistic interpretations about shunting (C84) and depolarization block (C85) are reasonable inferences from the electrophysiological data, though not directly demonstrated. The structure-function relationships linking kinetics to functional outcomes (C86-C88) are well-supported by the data.

result: The study leverages established principles of optogenetics and zebrafish neurobiology, including that optogenetics enables high spatio-temporal resolution manipulation of neural activity, stable expression systems offer advantages over transient ones, opsin efficacy depends on multiple factors including expression and cell properties, zebrafish provide genetic accessibility and transparency advantages, and optogenetic activation of trigeminal neurons reliably elicits escape responses.
evaluation: Claims C23-C27 represent established knowledge from prior literature, appropriately cited throughout the manuscript. These provide the scientific foundation and rationale for the study design. The claims are well-supported by the cited references and represent accurate characterization of the field.

result: The study appropriately applies established neurophysiological principles, including that photocurrent kinetics influence temporal precision of spike induction, primary motor neurons can spike at high frequencies (300-500 Hz), optogenetic high-frequency firing should be limited by opsin properties rather than cell physiology, embryos coil spontaneously at 24-27 hpf with minimal photomotor responses, Cl-/H+ pumps systematically induce hyperpolarization, and chloride reversal potential changes over development.
evaluation: Claims C34-C36, C38-C39, C44, and C49 represent established neurophysiological knowledge appropriately cited and applied to interpret the experimental results. These principles are well-supported by the cited literature and correctly inform the study design and interpretation.

result: Anion channelrhodopsins can silence cells via shunting as well as depolarization block depending upon the reversal potential of chloride in vivo.
evaluation: Claim C45 is supported by the electrophysiological data showing that GtACRs can both excite (in embryonic conditions with high ECl) and inhibit (in larval conditions with lower ECl) neurons. The dual mechanisms of shunting and depolarization block are reasonable inferences from the voltage-clamp and current-clamp data, though not independently demonstrated.

result: Future improvements and extensions are proposed, including that expression might be enhanced through codon optimization, trafficking sequences, alternative targeting systems, and reporter optimization, and that the approach could be extended to K+ channel-based silencers like PAC-K.
evaluation: Claims C66 and C89 are speculative about future work, citing relevant literature to support the feasibility of proposed improvements. These represent reasonable suggestions based on prior work in the field, but are not tested in this study. The claims appropriately acknowledge limitations and suggest directions for future research.

result: The developed platform enables efficient selection and calibration of optogenetic tools for in vivo neuroscience, allows opsin-specific optimization of light delivery parameters, revealed that equivalent stimulation regimes produce different adaptation rates affecting high-frequency firing control, and provides a resource for designing controlled experiments and benchmarking novel opsins.
evaluation: Claims C69-C71 and C90 represent summary statements about the utility and contributions of the study. These are supported by the comprehensive characterization across behavioral and electrophysiological assays. The observation about opsin-specific adaptation (C71) is well-documented in Figure 5. The overall contribution claims are justified by the scope and rigor of the work.

result: CoChR has been used to elicit single spikes in mouse pyramidal cells with 1 ms pulses at frequencies up to 50 Hz, demonstrating that thorough calibration in the cell type of interest in vivo is necessary for precise control of spike number and timing.
evaluation: Claim C77 cites prior work (Ronzitti et al., 2017) showing different CoChR performance in a different cell type, and C78 draws the appropriate conclusion that cell-type-specific calibration is essential. This reasoning is sound and supported by the observation that CoChR showed burst firing in zebrafish pMNs but single spikes in mouse pyramidal cells.
